entry.title: Chain batched Cards after each grade (#74)
entry.content:
Chain batched Cards after each grade (#74)

* Chain batched Cards after each grade until the batch is done

After a grade, the browser serves the next batched Card still due through
a per-card prepare route, skipping anything already answered elsewhere;
failed batch Cards are never attempted there. When none remains the batch
closes with Batch complete. Single reviews outside a batch behave as before.

* Serialize journey card creates behind their status round-trip

entry.title: Review opens the explanation first, then asks correct-or-incorrect (#73)
entry.content:
Review opens the explanation first, then asks correct-or-incorrect (#73)

A review shows the situation and the sentence with the target coloured.
An Explanation button opens the answer, explanation, and usage note; only
then do Correct (good) and Incorrect (again) appear. The scheduler is
untouched, and the journey marks one Card correct and the other incorrect.

entry.title: Reviews ask understood-or-not, with the target coloured (#72)
entry.content:
Reviews ask understood-or-not, with the target coloured (#72)

A review shows the situation and the sentence with the target word in a
different colour, then asks plainly whether it was understood. Yes maps to
good, no maps to again; the scheduler never sees a third option. Answer,
explanation, and usage note appear only afterwards as feedback. Colouring
is per segment with an uncoloured fallback when segments do not rejoin.

entry.title: Dispatch review sessions as a pumped batch job (#71)
entry.content:
Dispatch review sessions as a pumped batch job (#71)

POST /study/review-batch selects due reviews, records one row per card,
and returns 202 immediately. Each GET advances one card — banking reserves
without taking, so work-through serves with fresh permits through the
normal Review path. Failed cards stay due and listed. No daemon; progress
is client-pumped and resumable. The browser shows progress and works the
batch through the existing grade flow.

entry.title: Accept compound and copula-lemmatized targets by span containment (#70)
entry.content:
Accept compound and copula-lemmatized targets by span containment (#70)

Grammar targets are present when the span contains the detected form, and
constructions inside the span are the word's own morphology. Vocabulary
targets tile their span and match by concatenated lemma and reading, with
な-adjective stems meeting their だ-lemmatized tokens. The cards CLI
locates targets with the same rule; the prompt documents the whole-word
span. Implements 2.7 (with a gate correction) and specs 2.12.

entry.title: Split study into Learn and Review queues (#69)
entry.content:
Split study into Learn and Review queues (#69)

The server offers learn (first untaught new Card, stored teaching only)
and review (first due Card that is not an untaught new Card) as separate
session modes behind one filtered serve, with the mixed start kept. The
taught check is a read; nothing is prepared for a Card the mode skips.
The browser shows Learn new and Review buttons, and the journey walks
both filters including Learn's empty queue.

entry.title: Dispatch Learning Material generations in the background so a slow mo…
entry.content:
Dispatch Learning Material generations in the background so a slow model is recoverable (#63)

Study generation held one synchronous Responses call open against a 30s
timeout, so a ~35s generation always failed and the Card stayed
ungeneratable. Preparation hit the same wall in #49: dispatch with
background: true, return on the queued id, then poll GET
/v1/responses/{id} to a terminal status. timeoutMs now bounds one HTTP
call and completionTimeoutMs (5min, unmeasured upper bound) bounds the
generation. A poll that 404s is an offline failure, not a transport
failure. Provider-cancelled maps to cancelled. No checkpoint: a lost
poll still means a fresh dispatch on retry, exactly as today.

entry.title: Teach a new Card from a sentence written when it was made (#62)
entry.content:
Teach a new Card from a sentence written when it was made (#62)

First exposure called the provider, so the first thing a learner sees after
adding a Card was a twenty to thirty second wait and a paid request, for a
sentence nobody had chosen. A Card can now carry its own teaching
presentation, stored when it is created and served from the reserve that
prepare already checks before generating. Review is untouched: varying the
sentence is the point of a review.

Authored is not unvalidated. The presentation passes the same validator as
generated material, and is built here with the same analyzer the validator
uses, so a sentence that assembles locally is one the server will accept.

That validator refused every る-verb. It requires the supporting language to
be known, and the potential-form patterns match the める tail of a plain
る-verb, so a sentence teaching 詰める was rejected for leaning on 可能形 it
never used -- while plain form is the only form whose reading identifies the
Card. The detections sit entirely inside the target span, which makes them
the target word's own morphology rather than language the learner must
already have; the validator already made that exclusion for grammar targets
and now makes it for vocabulary ones. The detector is unchanged, so
Preparation is unaffected.

The pre-check in cards:add held its own copy of that rule and kept refusing
verbs the validator had started accepting. It mirrors the validator now, and
says which constraint a sentence missed rather than only that it failed.

phase-2.md said no authored fallback exists. It now distinguishes authored
from unvalidated, which is the property that actually matters.

zzzzz-phase6-compatibility gets a real time budget. It walks three surfaces
in three browsers and fits Playwright's 30s default only unloaded, which is
the same measurement that zz-phase2-study needed.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Put the reading over the kanji and bring the sentence down to a reada…
entry.content:
Put the reading over the kanji and bring the sentence down to a readable size (#61)

The presented sentence was set at up to 4.5rem, which magnified whatever
the platform fell back to and left the glyphs visibly rasterised, and it
carried no readings at all -- the learner had to already know the kanji the
Card is teaching them.

The material has carried readingSegments all along, and the validator
requires their written parts to rejoin into exactly the sentence, so ruby
built from them cannot drop or duplicate text. It was simply never
rendered.

A reading over a whole written form prints its okurigana twice: 広い reads
ひろい, so ruby over the segment shows い as writing and again above it. The
kana at each end belong to both, so splitFurigana trims the ones they agree
on, leaving 広 carrying ひろ and い standing as itself. お客 keeps its お for
the same reason. A segment whose reading is its own writing is kana already
and takes none: が over が is noise that only pushes the line apart.

The split is pure text handling rather than view code, so it lives in its
own module with tests, including that the written form is always
recoverable from the pieces.

Type comes down to clamp(1.5rem, 3.5vw, 2.25rem) with line-height 2.1, so
the readings have room above every line rather than only the first.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Compare a grammar form regardless of character width (#60)
entry.content:
Compare a grammar form regardless of character width (#60)

Re-filing the four idioms as Vocabulary Cards, then checking every live
Grammar Card in the deck, found four that could not be taught -- and none
of them was mine. The V1 migration created them:

  Card  Verb[せる・させる]     declared  Verb［せる・させる］
  Card  ~ても~なくても        declared  ～ても～なくても
  Card  すこしも~ない         declared  すこしも～ない
  Card  とか~とか            declared  とか～とか

The same constructions, differing only in whether the tilde and brackets
are halfwidth or fullwidth. Each would have stopped the session that
reached it, exactly as the six I created did. The guard added in #59 made
them visible; it did not cause them.

`comparable` now applies NFKC, which folds the bracket pair, and removes
tildes wherever they appear rather than only at the start. All 299 live
Grammar Cards are teachable, and the six undeclared forms are still
refused.

The four idioms are Vocabulary Cards now: 間が悪い and 元も子もない as
adjectives, 我ながら and 私としたことが as adverbs, each keeping the
derivation that makes it memorable. Vocabulary has no declared-form
constraint, so they are teachable without extending a list that also drives
Preparation's detector. 〜からには and 〜てこそ stay suspended.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Refuse a Grammar Card where it is created, not where it is studied (#59)
entry.content:
Refuse a Grammar Card where it is created, not where it is studied (#59)

Six Grammar Cards were created naming forms outside the declared set --
〜からには, 〜てこそ, and four idioms. POST /api/study/cards accepted every
one. The material validator refuses an undeclared form, but by then the
Card is stored, and the session that reaches it fails with
unsupportedGrammarTarget: one unteachable Card stops the whole queue. That
is what "Start next Card" was reporting, and a slow retry of it is what
surfaced as a 502.

createCard now asks the same question, through an injected
`grammarTargetSupported` so Study does not reach into learning-material.
The existing `invalidCard` failure carries it, naming the field.

Asking the same question meant making it one question. The declared forms
are written for a reader rather than for comparison: some carry the
placeholder tilde, some a parenthetical sense, some list alternates behind
a slash. `〜てしまう（縮約）` and `てしまう / ちゃう` are both declared, so a
literal comparison refused the plain `〜てしまう` -- which a browser test
caught, because it creates exactly that Card. A guard that disagrees with
the thing it guards is worse than no guard.

`supportsGrammarTarget` normalises once and is used by both the Card route
and the validator, so a Card that is accepted can always be taught. It
still refuses all six forms that caused this.

The six existing Cards are suspended in production rather than deleted;
what to do with the idioms is a separate decision.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Add an agent-assisted route from subtitles to Cards (#58)
entry.content:
Add an agent-assisted route from subtitles to Cards (#58)

Preparation splits into a local stage that is deterministic and free and a
provider stage that asks for per-candidate evidence under exact-set-equality
verification. These three scripts keep the first and replace the second with
an agent reading the episode, producing ordinary Cards through the ordinary
route: Study cannot tell which way they arrived.

subs:scan reads the SRTs, signs in, and prints every distinct form with its
tags, frequency and a cue, marking what the Known Word Bank or an existing
Card already covers. On the first episode that removed 168 of 423 distinct
words, which is the check no reader can do reliably against 1,437 entries.
It calls no provider and writes nothing.

subs:context shows every occurrence of given words with the cues either
side. A dictionary lists every sense and leaves you choosing; the
surrounding cues show the one in use and supply the example sentence with
it. It separated おごり (complacency) from 奢る (to treat), which the scan
listed apart and a headword would have merged.

cards:add posts a reviewed proposal file through POST /api/study/cards, the
route the browser uses, so canonical identity, deduplication and scheduling
stay with Study rather than being bypassed. An existing Card is reported as
`existing`, so re-running resumes a partial run.

The scripts deliberately do not filter on worth. An earlier version dropped
tokens tagged 名詞/接尾 before anything saw them, which silently hid 放題 --
the word behind the episode's central joke. They show everything with its
tags and leave the cut to the reader.

The document records the division of labour, the route, and what the tools
get wrong: readings are of the surface rather than the dictionary form, so
破れる comes back as われる and 無頓着 as むとんじゃく. That defect is not
confined to these scripts. projection.ts relationFor and known-vocabulary.ts
sameForm both compare lemma and reading as a pair, so an inflected
occurrence of a known word does not match; measured over ordinary
conversational Japanese, 12 of 34 words already in the Known Word Bank were
classified as gaps. Preparation over-reports its gap until that is fixed.

Proposal files and subtitles stay outside the repository, because their
usage notes quote subtitle text.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Let a session outlive the process that issued it (#57)
entry.content:
Let a session outlive the process that issued it (#57)

Every deploy asked for the password again. Sessions were held in a Map in
process memory, so a restart forgot every one of them; the seven-day
lifetime never mattered because a deploy always came first.

The cookie now carries its own expiry and a signature over it, keyed off the
configured password, so a fresh process recognises a session it never
issued. The password is already in the environment and stable across
restarts, so this needs no new configuration and no storage.

Rotating GAFU_ACCESS_PASSWORD now invalidates every outstanding session. The
Map did not do that: it kept honouring sessions issued under the old
password until they expired.

What is given up: logout revokes for as long as the process lives, but a
restart forgets the revocation, so a signed-out cookie would be honoured
again until its expiry. Reaching that requires having captured the cookie
before sign-out, since sign-out clears it. For a single-owner deployment
behind a password, with a bounded lifetime, that is a smaller cost than a
login on every deploy -- but it is a real one, so it is stated here and in
the code rather than left to be discovered.

Tests cover the case the Map failed: a cookie issued by one instance is
accepted by a separately constructed one, refused after the password
changes, refused when its expiry is edited without re-signing, and refused
once that expiry passes.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Stop asking for a candidate on punctuation (#56)
entry.content:
Stop asking for a candidate on punctuation (#56)

"provider returned canonicalKey !? : where !?: was supplied": the model
answered `!? :` for a token whose canonicalKey is `!?:`, inserting a space,
and that one candidate rejected its batch.

Kuromoji files an unrecognised run of symbols under 名詞/サ変接続, so `!?`,
`...` and `...♪` arrive as nouns and earn vocabulary candidates. With no
reading, their canonicalKey is punctuation plus the empty-reading colon --
`!?:`, `...♪:` -- which is exactly the kind of string a model tidies.
Subtitles are full of them.

Precomputing the key in #54 was necessary but not sufficient: supplying a
string does not stop a model reformatting one that looks like a typo. The
answer is not to ask. A token now earns a candidate only if its surface
contains a letter or a number, so punctuation is absent from the payload
and from what the answer is compared against.

The predicate lives with the expectations, so the payload, the per-batch
check, and the run-level check move together, and the fake providers use it
too rather than their own copy of contentParts.

promptVersion goes to preparation-v4. Two batches completed under v3 and
hold candidates v4 does not expect, which would read as invented evidence
at run level; completed batches are not re-checked, so they have to be
asked again.

Real words are unaffected, including those with no reading: グリズリー, Wi,
and 24 still earn candidates and still carry the trailing colon.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: Hold the API key only in the server environment (#55)
entry.content:
Hold the API key only in the server environment (#55)

The key was held in process memory and entered through settings, so every
restart discarded it. That is six re-entries across today's deploys, and it
made an environment-supplied key ambiguous: a key typed in settings won the
session and then silently reverted to the environment's on the next deploy,
while "Remove API key" cleared a copy that came back on restart.

The key is now a deployment value and nothing else. It is read from
OPENAI_API_KEY at startup, held in process memory, and verified against the
provider on first preflight. There is no route, form, or session copy that
could disagree with the environment.

Removed: PUT and DELETE /api/provider/key, replaceProviderKey and
removeProviderKey from the LearningMaterial seam, replace and remove from
ProviderKeyCustody, the settings form and its remove button, and the
revision counter that existed only to order concurrent replacements.
Settings now reports which provider and model are configured and whether
the environment supplied a key, and names OPENAI_API_KEY when it did not.

This keeps the phase-2 invariant that matters -- the key never reaches
SQLite, a backup, a response, or a log -- while dropping the browser entry
path that phase-2 also described. Railway stores it encrypted at rest and
can seal it so it is write-only, which is strictly better custody than a
value retyped into a form after every deploy.

phase-2.md is updated to match rather than left contradicting the code: the
custody bullet, the settings paragraph, the LearningMaterial type, and the
two adversarial cases that were about replacing and removing a key.

The Playwright harness supplies OPENAI_API_KEY, because the key can no
longer be entered through the page it is testing.

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
